review: The whole hymn is a chain of appositive titles with almost no verbs, exactly as the Arabic (أَنْتَ نَبْعُ … أَنْتَ مَوْضُوعُ … أَنْتَ تُرْسِي …). The Hebrew keeps the verbless equation in 1:2–1:4 and 3:1–3:4, because the psalm's own confession is a string of nouns with suffixes (Ps 18:2–3).

2:3–2:4 מָגִנִּי וּמִבְצָרִי … נִצָּחוֹן — the Arabic أَنْتَ تُرْسِي أَنْتَ حِصْنِي … كُلَّ نَصْر; the Hebrew keeps מָגֵן and מִבְצָר, the two nouns of Ps 18:3 (מָגִנִּי וְקֶרֶן־יִשְׁעִי מִשְׂגַּבִּי וּמְנוּסִי), rather than the Modern מָגֵן וְהַגָּנָה.

4:1–4:2 רוֹפְאִי … מְרַפֵּא כָּל־חֳלִי — the Arabic يَا طَبِيبِي وَالدَّوَاءُ / مُبْرِئٌ كُلَّ سَقَام is 'my physician and the cure, healing every sickness'; the Hebrew keeps the physician and the healing participle, with חֳלִי from Exod 15:26 (כָּל־הַמַּחֲלָה), so the line holds both the person and the act.

3:3–3:4 מוֹרִי וְתִקְוָתִי / מְקוֹר כָּל־שָׁלוֹם — the Arabic مُرْشِدِي أَنْتَ الرَّجَاءُ / مَصْدَرُ كُلِّ سَلَام places 'guide' and 'hope' in apposition and then 'source of peace'; the Hebrew keeps the three, so the stanza does not collapse the guidance into the peace.

1:2–1:3 מְקוֹר … מוֹשַׁע — the Arabic نَبْعُ … مَوْضُوعُ الرَّجَاءِ is 'fount … the theme of hope'; the Hebrew uses מוֹשַׁע ('salvation/help', Ps 18:3) for the second rather than a literal 'subject', because the line must still say what the Lord is to the singer.
